question:
Patient note:
A 91-year-old widowed woman who previously worked as a school librarian arrived to the internal-medicine intake clinic this morning in her daughter’s wheelchair van for a scheduled comprehensive review of her chronic cardiopulmonary symptoms before the upcoming winter, when she ordinarily relocates to her granddaughter’s home at higher altitude. She relates progressive fatigue over the past six months, describing that she now needs two pauses while crossing the length of her small backyard and has begun sleeping on three pillows to avoid waking short of breath, though she is still able to shuffle unaided to the bathroom at night. She has never been informed by any physician that she sustained a heart attack, and there is no record of prior myocardial infarction in her chart. Review of prior outside records shows a transthoracic echocardiogram performed nine months ago that documented a dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis, an end-diastolic dimension of 6.3 cm, and an ejection fraction of 35 %, accompanied by mild functional mitral regurgitation and an estimated pulmonary-artery systolic pressure of 48 mm Hg; at that visit she was started on carvedilol 3.125 mg twice daily and torsemide 20 mg each morning, medications she has taken regularly according to pharmacy refill logs kept by her daughter. She has never undergone coronary angiography, denies ever being rushed to an emergency department for crushing sub-sternal discomfort, and serial high-sensitivity troponin assays drawn during two remote admissions for volume overload were below the analytic cutoff, suggesting that her pump failure is more likely related to decades of untreated hypertension than to scar from an occlusive event. Her respiratory history antedates the ventricular dysfunction: she smoked unfiltered cigarettes from age 17 to 63, accumulating roughly 40 pack-years before quitting when her first great-grandchild was born. Office spirometry obtained two years ago revealed an FEV1 of 0.9 L (46 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52 and less than 5 % reversibility after inhaled albuterol, consistent with fixed obstructive physiology. She inhales tiotropium 18 µg each morning, fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 µg twice daily, and keeps levalbuterol in her apron pocket, using two puffs most evenings when folding laundry; she has required one five-day oral prednisone burst in the past year after a viral bronchitis but has never been intubated or placed on noninvasive ventilation. The patient reports no calf cramping on ambulation, no non-healing lower-extremity ulcers, and pedal pulses were recorded as palpable at her podiatry visit last month; she has never been diagnosed with peripheral arterial disease nor undergone any limb vascular procedure. Neurologic review is unrevealing: she balances her own checkbook, recognizes all grandchildren by name, and completes the daily newspaper crossword in pen, albeit more slowly than in earlier years; neither she nor her family recall episodes of sudden unilateral weakness, facial droop, speech arrest, brief blindness in one eye, or any prior stroke. She denies chronic abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, hematemesis, melena, or prior abnormal liver chemistry panels. Metabolic labs drawn four weeks ago showed fasting glucose 103 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.7 %; her clinicians have not labeled her as having diabetes, and she has never required antihyperglycemic medication. Last measured serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73 m², blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L. She has never experienced upper-gastrointestinal bleeding, never received a Helicobacter eradication course, and has never been told she has a peptic ulcer; she uses acetaminophen rather than non-steroidal agents for occasional arthralgia. She drinks half a glass of red wine on her birthday and Christmas only, and has never used illicit substances. She has no history of chronic liver disease, malignancy, leukemia, or HIV infection. Vaccinations are current for influenza, tetanus, pneumococcus, and shingles. Family history notes a sister who died at 83 from complications of pneumonia and a brother who succumbed to a cerebrovascular hemorrhage at 79; no first-degree relative underwent limb bypass or dialysis. Current medications, all taken prior to today’s visit, include carvedilol, torsemide, lisinopril 5 mg daily, tiotropium, fluticasone-salmeterol, levalbuterol as needed, calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily, cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily, and a baby aspirin each morning suggested by a prior primary physician; she reports swelling of the lips to sulfa antibiotics in her thirties and avoids that class. On examination she is a petite woman seated upright in a transport chair, breathing comfortably at rest yet engaging in frequent pursed-lip expirations. Vital signs: temperature 36.4 °C, blood pressure 122/64 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 80 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 94 % on room air, weight 52 kg, height 157 cm, yielding a body-mass index of 21 kg/m². Perioral cyanosis is absent, conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric. Neck inspection reveals jugular venous pulsation 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The apical impulse is displaced laterally to the sixth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line; S1 and S2 are soft, a faint holosystolic blowing murmur is audible at the apex, and a third heart sound follows the diastolic pause. Lungs exhibit markedly prolonged expiration with scattered end-expiratory wheezes and faint late-inspiratory crackles at both bases; percussion is diffusely hyperresonant. The abdomen is flat and nontender with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge is not palpable, and there is no shifting dullness or splenomegaly. Mild pitting edema is present to the mid-shin bilaterally; skin is warm with intact hair distribution, and posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are 1 +. Neurologic testing shows an alert, oriented elder with clear articulation, intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric 4+/5 strength in proximal muscles limited by fatigue, normal sensation to light touch, and a slow, broad-based gait that she attributes to deconditioning rather than vertigo. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained on arrival displays sinus rhythm at 78 beats/min, low voltage in limb leads, left-axis deviation, and nonspecific ST–T changes without pathologic Q waves. Portable chest radiograph demonstrates a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, flattened diaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Baseline laboratory panel drawn today reveals hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, white-blood-cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 244 × 10⁹/L, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 76 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. She requests guidance on whether her current breathlessness warrants an increase in diuretic dosage, clarification about the safety of traveling to 7,000 feet elevation with her portable oxygen concentrator (which she uses only during exertion at 2 L/min), and an updated medication list to share with the visiting home-health nurse who assists with pillbox organization twice weekly.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Use the age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), which adds age points to weighted chronic diagnoses present at intake.
- Age: 50–59 years scores 1, 60–69 scores 2, 70–79 scores 3, and ≥80 scores 4. At 91 years → +4.
- Congestive heart failure: LVEF 35% with orthopnea, edema and prior admissions for volume overload → +1. No separate myocardial infarction is documented.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: fixed airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC 0.52) requiring maintenance inhalers → +1.
- No other qualifying comorbidity is documented; HbA1c 5.7% does not establish diabetes, and eGFR 68 does not indicate moderate or severe renal disease → 0.
Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 6.
Final answer: 6
